theme: Naming the Brave: Duryodhana Counts Heroes
hindi: दुर्योधन द्रोणाचार्य से कहता है कि पांडवों की सेना में धृष्टकेतु, चेकितान, पराक्रमी काशिराज, पुरुजित्, कुन्तिभोज और मनुष्यों में श्रेष्ठ शैब्य जैसे वीर भी हैं।
english: Duryodhana goes on pointing out the Pandava warriors to Drona: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the mighty king of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya, the best among men.
deeper: This verse is simply a list of names, but a list can tell us how someone feels. Duryodhana is not calmly chatting. He is busy counting the strong people on the other side, one by one. When we feel unsure inside, we often count the strengths of others again and again.

The names also show how wide the Pandava side was. Kuntibhoja was the king who had raised Kunti, the Pandavas’ mother, as his own daughter. Shaibya was a king connected to Yudhishthira’s family by marriage. Kashi was a famous kingdom. Many good people had come to stand with the Pandavas, and Duryodhana could see it.

The gentle lesson is this: it is wise to know what you are facing, but not wise to let worry take over your heart. Preparation makes us steady. Fear only makes us restless. Keep this in mind as we read on, because Arjuna’s own heart will soon be shaken in a very different way.
words: Dhrishtaketu, a brave king of Chedi
mighty, full of strength and courage
Kuntibhoja, the king who raised Kunti
background: The great war of Kurukshetra is about to begin. Blind King Dhritarashtra has asked Sanjay what his sons and the Pandavas are doing on the battlefield (1.1). Sanjay tells him that Duryodhana saw the Pandava army arranged for battle and went straight to his teacher Drona (1.2).

Duryodhana points out the Pandava army and reminds Drona that it was arranged by Drupada’s son, Drona’s own student (1.3). He then begins naming great archers and chariot-warriors such as Yuyudhana, Virata and Drupada (1.4). In this verse (1.5), he keeps adding more names to the list.
lessons: It is sensible to look carefully at the challenge in front of you.
Counting only other people’s strengths can make our own heart shaky.
Many kind and brave people stood with the Pandavas, which shows how friendship and goodness attract support.
Seeing and naming what is good in others is a fine habit, even when they are on the other team.
Preparation helps us be calm; fear without preparation only makes us restless.
examples: Aarav kept checking how many marks his classmates usually got, and he forgot to revise. His mother said, “Know the test, but study your own pages.” He closed the list and opened his book.
Before a gully cricket match, Rohan noticed how many good batters the other team had. He told his friends, “Let’s practise our bowling instead of just worrying.”
Ananya heard that the girl before her had a beautiful voice. She took three slow breaths and thought about her own song. She sang calmly and enjoyed it.
Kabir looked at the swimmers in the next lanes and felt his stomach tighten. His coach said, “Look at the water in your own lane.” That helped him begin well.
Meera saw that other children had brought fancy colour boxes. She felt small for a moment. Then she remembered how much she had practised and began her drawing happily.
Before a school chess match, Sameer read about his opponent’s past wins. He learned a few useful things, then stopped reading and played his own game.
Priya listed the strengths of her teammates: Zoya draws well, Dev speaks well. Naming their strengths made her feel happy to be part of the team, not afraid.
Tara saw how tall and fast the runners from the next school were. She felt nervous but whispered to herself, “I’ve trained, and I’ll do my best.” She ran with a smile.

story.title: Nisha and the Quiz Team List
paras: Nisha was captain of her school’s quiz team in Pune. The day before the inter-school quiz, she got a paper listing the other teams. She began reading the names aloud: “This boy won last year. That girl knows all the science. This team has three champions!”
With each name, her voice grew smaller and her hands felt colder. Her friend Sanjana said, “Nisha, you have counted all of them twice. Have you counted us even once?”

Nisha stopped. Then she slowly said, “Sanjana remembers every date in history. Imran is quick with maths. Kavya never forgets a capital city.” As she named her own team, her shoulders relaxed. She still respected the other teams, but she was no longer shaking.

The next day, they did not win every round, but they answered bravely and helped each other. Walking home, Nisha smiled and said, “Knowing the other teams was useful, but practising together was better.”
story.moral: Lesson: Look at the challenge honestly, but spend more time preparing and trusting your own team than counting everyone else’s strengths.

quiz.q: What is Duryodhana doing in this verse?
o: Naming more brave warriors on the Pandava side
quiz.x: He keeps pointing out the strong warriors in the Pandava army to Drona.
Nara-puṅgava literally means ‘bull among men’, a way of saying the best of men.

o: The king who raised Kunti as his daughter
quiz.x: Kuntibhoja adopted and raised Kunti, the mother of the Pandavas.

quiz.q: What gentle lesson can we take from this list of names?
o: Know the challenge, but don’t let worry take over
quiz.x: Being aware helps us prepare, but worry alone makes us restless.

reel.hook: Ever counted everyone else’s strengths and forgotten your own?
reel.lesson: Know your challenge, but prepare calmly instead of letting worry grow.
reel.caption:
Duryodhana keeps naming the Pandava heroes, and it shows how worry can feel. 🛡️
Know what you face, then focus on your own preparation.
What will you practise today? 🌟
